title: Set 3 · Hurdles & tax shields
description: Priced risk, project rates, WACC, and interest deductions.

questions.prompt: Under CAPM, which exposure earns an expected risk premium?

options.text: Firm-specific risk that can be diversified away.
Every source of total return volatility equally.
Any risk that caused the investor a loss last year.

questions.explanation: CAPM compensates systematic exposure; diversifiable firm-specific risk earns no separate premium.
questions.detail: Investors can spread independent firm-specific risks across a broad portfolio. What remains relevant for CAPM compensation is how the investment covaries with the market, summarized by beta.
questions.misconception: A stock can be volatile because of firm-specific news without having a high CAPM expected return.

questions.prompt: Which discount rate should be used for a new project whose risk differs from the firm’s existing business?

options.text: A rate appropriate for the project’s risk and financing.
The firm’s existing average rate, regardless of the project’s risk.
The risk-free rate, since the firm can diversify.

questions.explanation: The required return must match the project’s risk and financing.
questions.detail: The opportunity cost of capital depends on the use of the funds. A single company-wide hurdle can accept overly risky projects too easily or reject attractive safer projects. Comparable businesses can help assess the project’s systematic risk.
questions.misconception: The identity of the parent company does not make all its projects equally risky.

questions.prompt: With sufficient taxable income, what does an additional deductible interest payment do to the corporate tax bill?

options.text: It reduces taxable income and therefore reduces corporate taxes.
It increases taxable income and therefore increases corporate taxes.
It has no effect on taxable income.
It always eliminates the entire corporate tax bill.

questions.explanation: Deductible interest lowers taxable income, creating an interest tax shield.
questions.detail: For a fully usable deduction, the annual tax saving is \(T_C\times\text{interest paid}\). The firm saves the tax rate times the deduction, not the full interest payment.
questions.misconception: A tax deduction reduces taxable income; it is not a dollar-for-dollar tax credit.

questions.prompt: What is the firm’s after-tax weighted average cost of capital?
questions.context: Using market values, the firm is financed 50% by equity and 50% by debt. Its cost of equity is 14%, cost of debt is 8%, and corporate tax rate is 25%. Assume interest is fully deductible. Enter a percentage.
questions.explanation: 10%: the equity contribution is 7%, and the after-tax debt contribution is 3%.
questions.detail: Use \(r_{WACC}=(E/V)r_E+(D/V)r_D(1-T_C)\), with \(V=E+D\). The after-tax debt cost is \(8\%(1-0.25)=6\%\). Weighting the two sources gives \(0.5(14\%)+0.5(6\%)=10\%\).
questions.misconception: Apply the corporate-tax adjustment to debt, not to equity. The weights use market values rather than book values.

questions.topic: Present value of the tax shield
questions.prompt: What is the present value of the interest tax shield, in millions of dollars?
questions.context: A firm maintains $80 million of permanent debt. Its corporate tax rate is 20%. Assume sufficient taxable income to use all interest deductions and tax-shield risk equal to debt risk. Enter the number of millions.
questions.detail: Under the stated permanent-debt assumptions, \(PV(\text{interest tax shield})=T_C D\). Thus \(0.20\times80=16\) million dollars. Equivalently, discounting the perpetual annual tax saving \(T_C r_D D\) at \(r_D\) yields \(T_C D\).
questions.misconception: Do not multiply by the interest rate again: that gives an annual tax saving, not the present value of all future tax savings.
